cases.question_text: During translation, how does AUG differ from the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA? Include the roles of start signals, amino-acid coding, and protein release factors. Explain what happens to the growing polypeptide and the ribosome when a stop codon is reached, instead of treating the stop codon as an instruction to add another amino acid.

financial_and_transport.deadline_anchor: normal transport case claim after startup prewarm before listener

response.answer_text: AUG differs from the stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA in that AUG both specifies the amino acid methionine and serves as the start codon that initiates translation [ev_004] [ev_006]. The reading frame is set by the AUG start codon near the 5' end of the mRNA, and the mRNA is then read in groups of three [ev_004] [ev_006]. In contrast, three of the 64 codons are stop codons, which terminate protein synthesis and release the polypeptide from the translation machinery [ev_004] [ev_006]. Stop codons are called nonsense codons, and they do not instruct the addition of an amino acid to the chain [ev_004] [ev_007]. When the ribosome encounters a stop codon, the growing polypeptide is released and the ribosome subunits dissociate and leave the mRNA [ev_002]. Termination occurs when a nonsense codon (UAA, UAG, or UGA) is encountered; upon aligning with the A site, these codons are recognized by protein release factors that resemble tRNAs [ev_007] [ev_001]. The releasing factors instruct peptidyl transferase to add a water molecule to the carboxyl end of the P-site amino acid, which forces that amino acid to detach from its tRNA, and the newly made protein is released [ev_001]. Entry of a release factor into the A site terminates translation and the components dissociate [ev_007]. The small and large ribosomal subunits then dissociate from the mRNA and from each other [ev_001].

cases.question_text: For a red blood cell whose membrane permits water movement but not movement of the relevant solutes, compare isotonic, hypertonic and hypotonic extracellular solutions. Describe net water movement and the resulting cell-volume changes. In an isotonic solution, does "no net water movement" mean individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane?

financial_and_transport.deadline_anchor: normal transport case claim after startup prewarm before listener

response.answer_text: For a red blood cell whose membrane is water permeable but not permeable to the relevant solutes, osmosis moves water according to its concentration gradient across the membrane, which is inversely proportional to the solutes' concentration [ev_006]. In that situation the solute cannot pass through the membrane, but the water can [ev_002].  In an isotonic solution, the extracellular fluid has the same osmolarity as the cell, and there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell [ev_004] [ev_001]; the cell keeps its normal volume and shape [ev_003]. In a hypertonic solution, the surrounding fluid has greater solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes out of the cell into the surrounding fluid and the red blood cell shrivels [ev_004] [ev_003]. In a hypotonic solution, the surrounding fluid has lower solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes into the red blood cell, causing it to swell and possibly rupture (lyse) [ev_004] [ev_003]. Water moves by osmosis, the diffusion of water through a semipermeable membrane, and the membrane limits the solutes' diffusion [ev_006] [ev_008]. Regarding your question: no. 'No net water movement' in an isotonic solution does not mean individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane; the source states there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell, although water will still move in and out [ev_004]. The source states that there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell, although water will still move in and out [ev_004].

response.answer_text: In the copper–silver galvanic cell, the anode is the copper electrode, where oxidation occurs (Cu to Cu2+) [ev_002]. The cathode is the silver electrode, where reduction occurs (Ag+ to Ag) [ev_002]. The spontaneous reaction produces Cu2+ cations in the anode half-cell and consumes Ag+ ions in the cathode half-cell [ev_001]. The source text does not explicitly state the direction of electron flow through the external wire, so I cannot confirm that direction from the supplied evidence; it is not established in these passages. The salt bridge is a tube filled with inert electrolyte solution that connects the two half-cell solutions, keeping the reactants separate while maintaining charge balance [ev_001]. As the reaction proceeds, NO3− flows in from the salt bridge to balance increasing Cu2+ in the anode half-cell, and Na+ flows into the cathode half-cell to compensate for decreasing Ag+ [ev_001]. Regarding charge carriers, the supplied evidence describes ions moving through the salt bridge but does not describe the charge carriers in the external wire, so that comparison cannot be completed from the current evidence.

cases.question_text: In bacterial DNA replication, explain why leading-strand synthesis is continuous while lagging-strand synthesis produces Okazaki fragments, including the direction in which new DNA is synthesized. How are RNA primers replaced and the remaining nicks between DNA fragments sealed?

financial_and_transport.deadline_anchor: normal transport case claim after startup prewarm before listener

response.answer_text: DNA polymerase can only extend a new strand in the 5' to 3' direction, so new DNA is synthesized only in the 5' to 3' direction [ev_006]. At the replication fork, one template strand is oriented 3' to 5' and the other 5' to 3' [ev_001]. The new strand complementary to the 3' to 5' parental strand can be synthesized continuously toward the replication fork; this is the leading strand [ev_001]. The other new strand, complementary to the 5' to 3' parental strand, is extended away from the replication fork in small fragments called Okazaki fragments, and each fragment needs its own primer to start synthesis; this is the lagging strand [ev_001] [ev_007]. The leading strand can be extended from a single primer, whereas the lagging strand needs a new primer for each short Okazaki fragment [ev_001]. The overall direction of the lagging strand is 3' to 5', and that of the leading strand is 5' to 3' [ev_002]. RNA primers are replaced by DNA as synthesis proceeds: DNA pol I removes the primers by its exonuclease activity, uses the DNA behind the RNA as its own primer, and fills the gaps with DNA nucleotides [ev_002]. The remaining nicks between the newly synthesized DNA and the previously synthesized DNA are sealed by DNA ligase, which forms phosphodiester linkages between the 3'-OH end of one nucleotide and the 5' phosphate end of the adjacent fragment [ev_002].

response.answer_text: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction, and it needs a free 3'-OH group to extend from [ev_006]. Because the two template strands are antiparallel, one new strand can be extended continuously toward the replication fork; this is the leading strand [ev_001] [ev_007]. The other new strand is synthesized away from the replication fork in short pieces called Okazaki fragments, and each fragment needs its own RNA primer to start synthesis; this is the lagging strand [ev_001] [ev_007]. The overall direction of the lagging strand is 3' to 5', and that of the leading strand is 5' to 3' [ev_002]. RNA primers are replaced by DNA as synthesis proceeds: DNA pol I removes the primers by its exonuclease activity, uses the DNA behind the RNA as its own primer, and fills the gaps with DNA nucleotides [ev_002]. The remaining nicks between the newly synthesized DNA and the previously synthesized DNA are sealed by DNA ligase, which forms phosphodiester linkages between the 3'-OH end of one nucleotide and the 5' phosphate end of the adjoining fragment [ev_002].
